claims.text: The stability of equimolar nanoparticles containing five or more metals as a single-phase solid solution is governed by the balance between configurational mixing entropy and differential atomic diffusion kinetics.
At approximately 473 K, high mixing entropy and limited atomic rearrangement maintain structural and chemical homogeneity.
At temperatures approaching 1923 K, increased atomic mobility can overcome stabilization of the homogeneous phase.
Elements with lower diffusion activation energies preferentially migrate and segregate at elevated temperature.

Nanoparticles containing elements with significantly different diffusion barriers will exhibit a temperature-driven onset of phase segregation or surface reconstruction relative to their pristine state.
Possible products of high-temperature reconstruction include intermetallic phases or oxides.
Differential diffusion activation energies among constituent metals mediate the transition from a homogeneous solid solution to a segregated or reconstructed phase.
At lower temperatures, configurational entropy maintains a metastable homogeneous phase despite minor differences in atomic size and bonding.
Elevated temperature increases atomic mobility and enables segregation of elements with lower diffusion barriers.
Competition between entropy-driven stabilization and kinetic diffusion limitations governs the operational stability range.
After treatment at approximately 473 K, the nanoparticles will retain a homogeneous solid-solution structure with minimal local compositional fluctuations.
After heating toward 1923 K, the nanoparticles will exhibit measurable elemental segregation, discrete domains, intermetallic compounds, or surface reconstruction relative to the initial state.
Oxide formation may occur during high-temperature treatment if the environmental conditions permit oxidation.
The proposed effect should hold when particle size, composition, and surface characteristics are controlled so that differential diffusion properties are the dominant variation.
Strong surface-energy effects or reactive atmospheres may cause deviations from the proposed behavior.
The onset temperature for significant segregation may vary with particle size, exact composition, and environmental conditions.
Surface oxidation may inhibit or accelerate segregation.
The controlled comparison consists of otherwise comparable nanoparticles annealed at 473 K and 1923 K under inert atmosphere, with a room-temperature sample as a control.

Persistence of a homogeneous single phase without significant segregation or secondary-phase formation after prolonged annealing at 1923 K, despite differing constituent diffusion barriers, would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
